_comment: The journal crawl's cost bounds. THESE LIVE HERE, NOT IN CODE (Prompt 5).
Discovery is fetch-and-classify: every candidate link costs one request,
so these two numbers are the entire difference between crawling a journal
and crawling a publisher. Changing them must not need a recompile.
max_pages: hard budget per journal. A crawl that stops here has NOT
covered the journal, and the outcome says so — see StoppedBy::Budget.
max_depth: 0 is the entry page alone; 3 is §3.4's stated bound.
author_services_hosts: publisher-wide guideline domains, which are not the
journal's own host but do carry its requirements. Allowlisted, never
inferred, because 'the publisher's domain' is not something a crawler can
derive from a URL without wandering.
journal_path_segments: how many leading path segments identify the JOURNAL
on a host that serves many. journals.plos.org/plosone/... is one;
frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/... is two; a host that serves one
journal is absent from this map and scopes to the whole host.
Measured: without it, a crawl of PLOS ONE wandered into PLOS Genetics,
PLOS Pathogens and PLOS Biology and spent one journal's budget on six;
and a crawl of The Lancet reached six sibling Lancet journals' homepages.
IT DOES NOT FIT EVERY PUBLISHER, and that is a limit of the approach
rather than a missing entry. Wiley identifies a journal by an id that
appears at varying path positions (/page/journal/10970258/... and
/journal/10970258/...), so no leading-segment prefix isolates it; SAGE's
entry path (/author-instructions/JHP) names the SECTION first and the
journal second. Both are left absent, which scopes them to the whole
host and shows up as off-journal pages in the crawl list — visible,
which is the property that makes this rule acceptable at all.
